newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Restrained distillate build seen in APIs.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Restrained distillate build seen in APIs.

text.p: Tuesday's oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) may show a restrained build in distillate stocks of less than one million barrels due to a focus on gasoline output and high demand.
"We could get only a small build in distillates because refiners focused on gasoline production after the cracks strengthened two weeks ago," said Rita Beale, analyst with Fimat USA Futures.
In a Reuters survey, traders expect distillate stocks to be unchanged to up one million barrels.

Analysts and dealers also said the inventory data, which measures stocks as of November 8, will reflect increased demand for heating oil, a component of distillate stocks, in preparation for this week's cold spell in the U.S. Northeast.

Gasoline stocks were seen growing between 500,000 and two million barrels after the gasoline-to-crude crack, a measure of refinery profitability, increased to $4.51 a barrel November 4 from $3.43 a barrel October 28.
"I would also expect an increase in (gasoline) imports," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. Gasoline imports for the week ended November 1 fell 14,000 barrels from the week ago.
Crude was seen down 1.5 million barrels to up one million barrels in an inventory shift from the data last week which showed a surprising 9.3 million barrel build.

Refinery utilization rates were seen about unchanged to down 0.5 percentage point. Sweeney Oil trader Jim Ritterbusch said seasonally, runs have been unchanged at this time of year in nine out of the past 10 years.

Dealers noted refineries were running at a feverish 93.9 percent, so crude could post a draw. Moreover, the arbitrage for North Sea Brent remains closed, and Ritterbusch expects imports to remain around a low seven million barrels a day.
Some dealers noted that refineries are emerging from seasonal turnaround when they shifted production focus to distillate from gasoline in preparation for the winter.

This keeps production rates high, especially distillate output which, as of November 1, was 3.6 million barrels a day, just below the record 3.8 million. Amid high output, William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown, said distillate stocks could grow about 2.5 million barrels or more.
"If we grew that much, we will have grown stocks enough for the winter. We could see flat stocks after that," said Brown.
